# Assembly

This is an unbuilt prototype. The hinge is one purchased brass hinge held by flush screws.
The thumbwheels are bought solid gears, and every arbor, shaft, bushing and the crown come
finished from a CNC-turning kit, so nothing in the movement is cut, measured or soldered: each
part is pushed on until it stops, with a drop of Loctite. The only soldering is electrical (the
carrier PCB and the speaker and mic leads, which plug into the carrier). Read the fabrication hold
and joint status below before buying parts.

**Animated version.** Every step below is also an animation in the design viewer
([`viewer/`](viewer/README.md), **Assemble** tab), showing each part moving into place, what
gets applied where, and the tools. This file is generated from
[`assembly/steps.yaml`](assembly/steps.yaml); edit that and run `python hardware/assembly/guide.py`.
[`assembly/FINDINGS.md`](assembly/FINDINGS.md) records the design review that shaped this order.

**Tests as you go.** Steps marked *Test* are checkpoints: do them before going on, because each one
is the last moment the parts it checks are easy to reach. Each says what passes and what to adjust
if it doesn't; §11 collects them. The gear meshes are designed with 0.22–0.28 mm of backlash, and
every laser-cut gear has a looser spare in the order (marked with a small hole in its rim) for a
pair that binds (`cad/mesh.py` checks every pair, including a worst-case laser cut).

**Conventions.** "Up" is toward the dial. Positions along a shaft are measured from the
**bottom face of P1** (the movement base plate). Every dimension comes from
[`cad/design.py`](cad/design.py). If you change the design, re-run `cad/build.py` and
the guide script.

| Level | Height above P1 bottom | What lives there |
|---|---|---|
| P1 (base plate) | 0 – 1.6 | tube bushings for every shaft |
| L0 | 2.1 | hand-I gear + sensor-I gear; bottom of all knob stacks |
| L1 | 4.1 | hand-II gear + sensor-II gear |
| L2 | 6.1 | hand-III gear + sensor-III gear (knob stacks end at 7.1) |
| L3 | 8.1 | needle gear + X27 motor gear |
| P2 (dial plate) | 9.6 – 11.2 | top bushings, cannon, dial sticker |

Above the dial (measured from the top of P2): cannon tip +0.35, needle +0.45, hand III +1.61,
hand II +2.34, hand I +3.07, cap +3.46 (top of cap +4.47). The crystal's underside sits at +6.0.
You never measure these: every height is set by a shoulder or a flush end on the turned parts.

## Tools and consumables

The full tool list, with the step that uses each tool, is in
[BOM.md §G](BOM.md#g-tools); consumables are in [BOM.md §E](BOM.md#e-dial-finish-and-consumables).
The one to get right is the countersink: a **90° zero-flute** cutter, not an 82° one.

## 0. Before you order

**Hinge fabrication hold.** The purchased hinge in CAD is a reference, not a verified supplier
model. Guden's [BR05050404-72 drawing](https://www.guden.com/itemdetail/BR05050404-72) specifies
.040" sheet, a .091" pin, .500" knuckle pitch and 1.060" open width, but not the curl/leaf offset
or knuckle-slot clearance. Obtain a sample or a complete drawing first, together with a quote for
the cut piece (§3.7). Confirm the five-knuckle cut, retained pin and trimmed leaf heights; update
the CAD pivot to match before ordering the case. The current model's 0.1 mm curl and slot
clearances are assumptions, not vendor tolerances. The opening limit is set by the hinge's own
leaves closing on each other (§9), so the real curl also sets that angle.

1. Generate the dial with Myth Made's symbols (see [`dial/README.md`](dial/README.md)). Print
   `dial/local/dial_print_letter.pdf` at 100 % on plain paper and check the 50 mm bar.
   It confirms the printer scale before you buy sticker stock.
2. Upload the files in `out/sendcutsend/` and check the instant quote (see *Ordering* in
   [README.md](README.md)). The `_L` gears are the mesh-tuning spares: order them with the rest.

## 1. Prepare the laser-cut parts

### 1.1 Deburr and flatten

Deburr and flatten everything. Rub each face on 600 grit on glass, then finer.
Gears only need their faces deburred; don't round the teeth.

*Apply:*

- 600–2000 grit on glass: both faces of every flat part
- 600–2000 grit on glass

*Tools:*

- 600–2000 grit wet-and-dry paper on a flat glass plate
- needle files

### 1.2 Test: Measure the gears

Before anything is glued, measure the tip diameter of one 32T gear and the 17T and 34T gears
with calipers, across opposite teeth (or over two teeth and a gap on the 17T). Nominal:
**27.2 mm** (32T), **15.2 mm** (17T), **28.8 mm** (34T). A cut that comes out large has
fat teeth everywhere in the order, and that is what makes a mesh bind. Look over every tooth
for a burr or a stuck dross bead at the root.

Keep the spares with an extra **Ø0.5 mm hole in the rim** (`_L` in the order) separate: they
have 0.16 mm thinner teeth.

*Apply:*

- Measure: tip Ø 27.2 mm (32T)
- Measure: tip Ø 15.2 mm (17T)

*Tools:*

- digital calipers
- 10× loupe

*Check:*

- Tip diameters within +0.06 / -0.10 mm of nominal
- No burrs or beads on the teeth

*If it fails:*

- Over +0.06 mm: expect tight meshes; plan to fit the `_L` spares for the gear-to-gear pairs (hand/sensor and needle) and confirm on the dry run (§3.1)
- Burr or bead: remove with a fine needle file along the tooth, not across it

### 1.3 Countersink the case screw seats

**Flush case screw seats, after forming.** The supplier DXFs and `__formed.step` files
retain plain through-holes. On the outside of the lower tray, countersink its three floor
holes (Ø2.7 mm); on the outside of the upper shell, its four top holes (Ø2.7 mm) and the two
small crystal-screw holes (Ø1.8 mm, either side of the window, just inside the grille ring).
Use **90° DIN 963 slotted countersunk brass screws**, not raised/oval countersunk or
larger-headed ISO alternatives. Work by hand with the thin sheet firmly supported, and test
the actual screw frequently until its head is flush, not below the surrounding face.
Countersink each M2 hole until its rim measures **Ø3.8–3.9 mm** (about 0.55 mm deep,
leaving about **0.47 mm** of straight hole in the 1.016 mm sheet), and each M1.6 hole to
**Ø3.0–3.1 mm**, then drop a screw in and check it sits flush. Light pressure, a few turns
at a time: the cutter centres itself in the existing hole. Stop as soon as the head is flush.
The hinge holes in the walls come laser-cut and are not countersunk (the leaves are).
Clean off chips and deburr before fitting any electronics.

*Apply:*

- Countersink 90°: 3 floor holes, outside
- Countersink 90°: 4 top holes, outside
- Countersink 90°: 2 crystal-screw holes, M1.6

*Tools:*

- 90° zero-flute countersink + T-handle
- digital calipers

*Check:* Rims Ø3.8–3.9 mm (M2) and Ø3.0–3.1 mm (M1.6); a screw dropped in sits flush

### 1.4 Glue the bushings into P1 and P2

No shaft runs in a laser-cut hole. Each plate hole takes a turned bushing exactly as thick
as the plate (§2), and its shaft slides inside it with about 0.08 mm of play, so every shaft
is located precisely whatever the laser tolerance. One end of each bushing's bore is
chamfered: fit them **chamfer down** (the collars sit on the plain end).

Lay P1 on a flat glass plate. Put a dab of Loctite 638 on each of its seven bushings and drop
it into its hole until it touches the glass: it is then flush both sides. The plate holes are
drawn 0.1 mm over the bushing, so they go in by hand. Do the same with P2's six, on the glass
beside it, then go straight on to the next step while the 638 is wet (it takes about 10
minutes to grab).

*Apply:* Loctite 638: outside of each bushing; chamfer down

*Tools:*

- flat glass plate
- tweezers

*Design review:* [F1: Bushing alignment procedure can't be followed as written](assembly/FINDINGS.md#f1)

### 1.5 Line up the bushing pairs with drill blanks

Screw P1 onto its three **M2×12 F-F** bay standoffs and the short **M2×4 F-F** corner standoff
with the four **M2×8 M-F** gear standoffs from above. Lower P2 (with its wet bushings) onto the
gear standoffs and screw the four **M2×5 M-F** hand standoffs through it.

Slide a **1/8" drill blank** through each sensor bushing pair and a **5/32" blank** through each
knob pair, from the top through both plates: each blank lines its two bushings up as the 638
cures. Spin each blank once, then leave the frame standing on its standoffs for an hour.

*Apply:* Loctite 638: P2's bushings, glued on the glass; chamfer down

*Tools:*

- 3 × 1/8" and 3 × 5/32" drill blanks (gauge pins)
- 4 mm nut driver

*Check:* Each blank slides through its pair without forcing

*Design review:*

- [F1: Bushing alignment procedure can't be followed as written](assembly/FINDINGS.md#f1)
- [F8: The crown corner was held by a loose nut](assembly/FINDINGS.md#f8)

### 1.6 Take P2 off again

Once the 638 has cured, pull the drill blanks out, unscrew the hand standoffs and lift P2 off.
P1 stays on its standoffs: it is the movement frame from here on.

## 2. Check the turned-parts kit

Nothing to cut. The kit arrives finished; [`out/turned/README.md`](out/turned/README.md) is its
drawing (also `out/turned/turned_parts.csv`). Unpack it onto a tray and check each part's
length with calipers against that table, so you know which is which:

| Part | Qty | What sets its position |
|---|---|---|
| `arbor_I` (stepped rod) | 1 | Its collar rests on P1's centre bushing; gear I sits on the collar; hand I sits on the top shoulder; the cap is flush with the top |
| `arbor_II`, `arbor_III`, `arbor_needle` (plain tubes) | 1 each | Gear flush with the bottom end, hand flush with the top end |
| `cannon` (flanged tube) | 1 | Flange on P2's top face |
| `bushing_1_8`, `bushing_5_32`, `bushing_3_16` | 1, 6, 6 | Flush with both faces of the plate, chamfered end down |
| `shaft_sensor_I/II/III` | 1 each | Collar on the P1 bushing (0.5, 2.5 and 4.5 mm tall: the gear sits on it); top tip chamfered |
| `magnet_cup` | 3 | Pushed onto the sensor shaft's bottom tip until it stops |
| `shaft_knob` | 3 | Collar on the P1 bushing; the thumbwheel sits on it; top tip chamfered, 0.6 mm proud of P2 |
| `sleeve_knob` | 3 | Slides down onto the thumbwheel |
| `crown_turned` | 1 | E-clip in its groove inside the wall |

Check the chamfers are there: the knob shafts are the longest shafts so that P2 picks them up
first (§6). The **hinge body backing** (.063" brass, 63.5 × 11 mm) comes laser-cut with the
SendCutSend order.

## 3. Dry run and sub-assemblies

### Mechanical joint status

Prefer removable mechanical joints wherever practical, rather than automatically replacing
solder with permanent adhesive. Current construction of every joint:

| Joint | Current construction |
|---|---|
| Hinge knuckles and pin | One purchased formed hinge, supplied cut to length and trimmed. Supplier fit is still on hold above. |
| Hinge to body/lid | Flush countersunk screws from outside; nuts on a backing strip (body) or washers (lid) inside; removable. |
| Opening stop | None added: the hinge leaves close on each other just past flat. |
| Crystal and spiders | Two M1.6 countersunk screws through the top face, nuts under the seat spider; removable. |
| Thumbwheels | One bought solid gear each, on the knob-shaft collar, Loctite 638. |
| Sensor, hand and needle gears | On a turned collar or flush with a tube end, Loctite 638 (no solder). |
| Cannon | Flanged; pushed into P2's 0.1 mm-clearance hole, Loctite 638. |
| Crown | One turned piece, held by a DIN 6799 E-clip; removable. |
| Speaker and mic leads | Soldered at the speaker and mic; plug into PicoBlade headers J5 / J4 on the carrier. |
| Bushings, hands, magnets, magnet cups | Loctite 638 / epoxy; not designed to be taken apart. |

Do not put ordinary radial set screws directly into the thin nested hand tubes: denting them
can bind the adjacent arbor.

Every gear goes on the same way: a drop of Loctite 638 on the shaft, slide the gear down until it
stops, wipe off the excess and keep it out of any bore. Leave each one an hour before handling.
Loctite 638 lets go at about 250 °C: a soldering iron held on the part for 20–30 s releases a
gear or bushing that has to come off. Clean both parts back to bare metal before refitting.

### 3.1 Test: Dry-run the gear train

Before anything is glued, put the whole hand train together dry and turn it. Gear bores are
drawn only 0.08 mm over the turned diameter, so each gear runs centred; if one won't slide
on, turn the matching drill through it by hand.

Slide each gear onto its shaft or arbor without glue: thumbwheels onto the knob shafts, sensor
gears onto the sensor shafts, hand gears onto the arbors. Nest the arbors in P1's centre
bearing, stand the sensor and knob shafts in their bushings, slide the sleeves on, lower P2 and
screw the hand standoffs in. Then turn each thumbwheel through **two full turns** each way
(its hand goes round 1.6 times), slowly, feeling for a tight spot; and hold each hand gear
still and rock its sensor gear to feel the play. Loose gears may slip on their shafts here:
that doesn't matter, it's the teeth you're testing.

*Apply:*

- Check: two full turns each way
- Check: rock against the held hand gear

*Check:*

- Every thumbwheel turns its train through two full turns with an even, light feel
- A just-visible rock (about 1°) between each pair, everywhere round
- Turning one knob doesn't move the other two hands

*If it fails:*

- Tight spot or binding in one pair: swap the laser-cut gear of that pair for its `_L` spare (sensor gear for knob → sensor, hand gear first for sensor → hand) and try again; swap both if it still binds
- Every pair tight: the order was cut fat (§1.2); fit the `_L` sensor and hand gears throughout
- A train drags without a tight spot: a shaft is rubbing in a bushing; turn it alone, and if it is the bushing pair, release the 638 with heat and redo §1.5 for that pair
- A knob moves another hand: gears on neighbouring levels are touching; check each sits on its collar or flush with its tube end

### 3.2 Thumbwheels (×3)

Each is one bought brass gear (module 0.8, 26 teeth, 5 mm wide, 4 mm bore; see BOM.md §C).
Slide it down a `shaft_knob` until it sits on the collar. No layers to align.

*Apply:* Loctite 638: on the shaft above the collar

### 3.3 Sensor shafts (×3)

Slide each 32T sensor gear (the one that passed the dry run) down its shaft until it sits on
the collar (I has the 0.5 mm collar, II 2.5 mm, III 4.5 mm). The magnet cup goes on later
(§5), once the shaft is in its bearings, because it's wider than the bearing hole.

*Apply:* Loctite 638: above each collar

### 3.4 Arbors

Stand arbors II and III and the needle arbor on end on a sheet of glass. Slide each gear down
until it touches the glass: it is then flush with the bottom end. Hand-II gear on `arbor_II`,
hand-III gear on `arbor_III`, the 17T needle gear on `arbor_needle`. The hand-I gear goes on
`arbor_I` from the thin top end and down onto its collar.

*Apply:*

- Loctite 638: bottom end of each tube
- Loctite 638: above arbor I's collar

*Tools:* flat glass sheet

### 3.5 Cannon into P2

Push the cannon into P2's centre hole from the top until its flange sits on the plate, with a
little Loctite 638 on the outside only. The needle arbor runs inside it.

*Apply:* Loctite 638: outside of the cannon only

### 3.6 Motor gear onto the X27

The 34T gear sits on the X27's **Ø1 output shaft**, with its bottom face 5.5 mm above the
motor's front face (level L3). Press it on with a drop of Loctite 638 and trim the shaft
0.3 mm above the gear. Don't push hard on the shaft; support it from behind.

*Apply:*

- Loctite 638: one drop on the Ø1 shaft
- Check: trim the shaft 0.3 mm above the gear

*Caution:* Support the motor body from behind; pushing on the shaft alone can damage its internal stop

### 3.7 Hinge: check it and drill the leaves

The hinge comes from Guden cut to five knuckles (63.5 mm, both end knuckles on the fixed leaf),
pin staked, lid leaf trimmed to 5.6 mm from the pivot (§0). The laser-cut `hinge_gauge` checks
that and drills the leaves:

1. Lay the hinge closed and flat on a scrap of wood, barrel up, and drop the gauge over it so
   the barrel sits in its slot. The slot ends should meet the cut ends of the barrel, and the
   lid leaf's edge should line up with the gauge's top edge.
2. Clamp the gauge to the hinge and drill through its six holes: four **Ø2.4 mm** in the
   fixed (case) leaf, two **Ø1.8 mm** in the lid leaf. They match the holes laser-cut in the
   case and lid.
3. Unclamp, deburr, and countersink the six leaf holes from the outside with the same 90°
   countersink until the screw heads sit flush: rim **Ø3.8–3.9 mm** on the M2 holes,
   **Ø3.0–3.1 mm** on the M1.6 holes.

If you cut the hinge from stock yourself instead, the same gauge marks it: cut across the
barrel at the slot ends, right in the knuckle joints, centre-punch the pin ends, and scribe and
file the lid leaf to the gauge's top edge.

*Apply:*

- Check: slot ends at the barrel's cut ends
- Drill: four Ø2.4 mm through the gauge (case leaf)
- Drill: two Ø1.8 mm through the gauge (lid leaf)
- Countersink 90°: leaf holes

*Tools:*

- drill with Ø1.8 mm and Ø2.4 mm bits
- two small clamps
- 90° zero-flute countersink
- digital calipers

*Check:*

- Slot ends meet the barrel's cut ends; lid leaf edge on the gauge's top edge
- All six leaf countersinks let a screw sit flush

*If it fails:*

- Lid leaf proud of the gauge edge: file it to the edge
- Cut a knuckle short or long: ask the supplier for a new piece

*Design review:*

- [F6: Six hinge holes were hand-drilled through the finished case](assembly/FINDINGS.md#f6)
- [F7: The hinge was cut from 72-inch stock by hand](assembly/FINDINGS.md#f7)

## 4. Carrier PCB and bench test (before anything goes in the case)

### 4.1 Populate the carrier

Populate the carrier per [`pcb/README.md`](pcb/README.md#assembly-order): resistors, C1, pin
headers, the two PicoBlade headers J4 (mic, 5 pins) and J5 (speaker, 2 pins), then the module
sockets, using each module as its own soldering jig. Solder the X27's two 1×4 sockets with the
rest: the motor mesh is set by the board's hole positions, like every other mesh. The crown
switch, power switch and battery socket J8 are soldered to the board too.

*Apply:* Solder (electrical): every through-hole joint from below, X27 sockets included

*Tools:*

- temperature-controlled soldering iron
- flush cutters
- multimeter

*Design review:*

- [F3: The motor mesh was set by solder-joint play, using the carrier as a jig](assembly/FINDINGS.md#f3)
- [F5: Speaker and mic leads were soldered in with the movement dangling beside the tray](assembly/FINDINGS.md#f5)

### 4.2 Plug in the modules and the wall USB-C board

Plug the ProS3, the DRV8833, the MAX98357A and the three AS5600 boards into their sockets.
Solder the cut end of the short USB-C cable (red, white, green, black) into J7 and plug it
into the ProS3.

The wall USB-C breakout stands on its 8-pin socket and two 5 mm nylon spacers; fix it with
two **M2×10** cheese-head screws from the top and M2 nuts under the carrier.

*Apply:* Solder (electrical): USB-C cable into J7

*Tools:*

- soldering iron
- 30 AWG wire stripper
- slotted screwdriver 1.5–2.5 mm
- 4 mm nut driver

### 4.3 Test: Bench test

Work through the [bring-up checklist](pcb/README.md#bring-up-checklist) one module at a
time. Flash the firmware (see [`../firmware/README.md`](../firmware/README.md)) once the
ProS3 is in, then check `hands`, `home`, `sweep`, `tone` and `rec` from the serial console,
probing the test pads if anything misbehaves. Turning a magnet over each AS5600 should walk
through all 36 symbols. Plug the X27 into its sockets for `home` and `sweep`, then take it out
again: it goes in through P1 in §6.

Run `wifi` and **write down the setup-portal password** it prints. Once the board is
inside the case you'll need it.

*Apply:*

- Check: turn a magnet over each AS5600
- Check: flash and test over USB

*Tools:*

- USB-C data cable + computer with PlatformIO
- multimeter
- a spare Ø6 mm magnet

*Check:*

- `hands`, `home`, `sweep`, `tone` and `rec` all pass
- Setup-portal password written down

*If it fails:* Follow the bring-up checklist's per-module checks and test pads (pcb/README.md)

## 5. Movement on the bench

The movement is built on P1 standing on its bay standoffs, and goes into the case in §6 as a frame
with its arbors and shafts. The X27, P2, dial and hands are fitted in the case: the X27's motor
gear cannot pass through P1's slot (see [F9](assembly/FINDINGS.md#f9)).

### 5.1 Nest the arbors

Nest arbors I, II and III and the needle arbor in the centre bearing, in that order, each
sliding over the last.

### 5.2 Drop in the sensor and knob shafts

Drop in the three sensor shafts, gears already on their collars, then the three knob shafts,
thumbwheels already on their collars. Slide a `sleeve_knob` down onto each thumbwheel.

### 5.3 Magnets

Push a Ø6×2.5 diametric magnet into each `magnet_cup` with a little epoxy until it bottoms.
Then, from underneath, put a drop of Loctite 638 on each sensor shaft's thin bottom tip and
push a cup on until it stops on the shoulder, while you hold the shaft down from above. The
cup then hangs 0.3 mm below P1 and the magnet is centred automatically.

*Apply:*

- 5-minute epoxy: in each cup's pocket
- Loctite 638: each sensor shaft's thin bottom tip

*Check:* Each sensor shaft still turns freely, with a little up-and-down play

### 5.4 Speaker

Solder a 2-way PicoBlade pigtail (~10 cm, pre-crimped) to the speaker's back tabs, thread it
down through the open centre of P1's speaker seat (top-left) and seat the speaker on its foam
ring. The seat is a ring so the speaker's back can breathe into the bay below.

*Apply:* Solder (electrical): 2-way pigtail to the back tabs (red to +)

*Tools:* soldering iron

*Design review:* [F5: Speaker and mic leads were soldered in with the movement dangling beside the tray](assembly/FINDINGS.md#f5)

### 5.5 Microphone under P2

Solder a 5-way PicoBlade pigtail (~10 cm) to the INMP441 (VDD GND SCK WS SD, with L/R bridged
to GND at the mic) and stick it under P2's 7-hole mic port, port up, with foam tape that has a
hole over the port. Its lead hangs down through P1's open lattice once P2 goes on.

*Apply:*

- Solder (electrical): 5-way pigtail; bridge L/R to GND
- Double-sided foam tape: hole over the mic port

*Tools:* soldering iron

*Design review:* [F5: Speaker and mic leads were soldered in with the movement dangling beside the tray](assembly/FINDINGS.md#f5)

## 6. Movement into the case

### 6.1 Carrier into the lower tray

Line the floor with one layer of Kapton. Put the three nylon spacers over the floor holes and
lower the populated carrier straight in: U7's receptacle lines up with the wall opening, the
crown switch goes into the top-right corner, and the power switch's slider lines up behind its
slot in the back wall. Fit the crown afterwards: its stem reaches about 1 mm over the board's
edge, so the carrier can't be lowered past it.

*Apply:* Kapton tape: one layer over the floor

*Design review:* [F10: The crown stem blocks the carrier if the crown goes in first](assembly/FINDINGS.md#f10)

### 6.2 Crown

Push `crown_turned` in from outside through the lower tray's top-right chamfer hole and snap
the DIN 6799 E-clip into its groove from inside (flat-nose pliers or an E-clip applicator),
between the wall and the crown switch. The groove's position gives the 0.3 mm of play.

*Tools:* flat-nose pliers or E-clip applicator

*Check:* The crown clicks the switch and springs back

*Design review:* [F10: The crown stem blocks the carrier if the crown goes in first](assembly/FINDINGS.md#f10)

### 6.3 Battery

Stick the cell down with thin double-sided foam tape and plug it into J8. Check with a meter
first that its red wire lands on the **+** mark: JST-PH polarity isn't standardised.

*Apply:* Double-sided foam tape: under the cell

*Tools:* multimeter

*Check:* Red lead on J8's + mark (measure before plugging in)

### 6.4 Plug in the speaker and mic leads

With P1's frame and P2 standing beside the tray, plug the speaker lead into **J5** and the mic
lead into **J4**: both headers sit right under their pass-throughs (see WIRING.md, *Where
things go*). They are covered by P1 from the next step on; the leads are long enough to lift
the movement out again and unplug them.

*Apply:*

- Plug in: speaker lead into J5
- Plug in: mic lead into J4

*Design review:* [F5: Speaker and mic leads were soldered in with the movement dangling beside the tray](assembly/FINDINGS.md#f5)

### 6.5 Lower the movement frame onto the carrier

Lower P1's frame straight down onto the carrier, threading the mic lead through P1's lattice.
The magnet cups come to rest just above the AS5600 chips. Fix it with three **M2×8
countersunk** screws from under the floor, through the spacers and board into the bay
standoffs.

*Tools:* slotted screwdriver 2.5 mm

### 6.6 Test: X27 in through P1's slot

Lower the X27 (motor gear on) through P1's slot into its sockets. The motor gear slides into
mesh with the needle gear (rock the needle arbor a hair if the teeth butt). Then, with USB
connected, run `home` and `sweep` and watch the needle gear: it should follow smoothly in both
directions. Gently rock the needle arbor with tweezers: you should feel a little play.

*Apply:* Check: `sweep`, then rock the needle arbor

*Check:*

- The X27 sits fully down in its sockets
- `sweep` runs smoothly both ways without the motor buzzing or skipping
- A little rock at the needle gear (about 1.5°)

*If it fails:*

- Buzzing, stalling or a tight spot: lift the X27 out, turn the needle arbor alone (it must spin freely); if it does, the pair is tight: release the needle gear with heat and fit `gear_needle_17T_L`, or press the `gear_motor_34T_L` onto the shaft
- No play at all: as above; too much (needle wanders by more than half a symbol): the order was cut thin, keep the standard gears and rely on calibration
- Needle moves the wrong way on `sweep`: set `MOTOR_PHASE_DIR = -1` in firmware/src/config.h

*Design review:*

- [F3: The motor mesh was set by solder-joint play, using the carrier as a jig](assembly/FINDINGS.md#f3)
- [F9: The motor gear can't pass P1's slot, so the movement can't be finished on the bench](assembly/FINDINGS.md#f9)

### 6.7 Lower P2 onto the shaft tips

Lower P2 over the cannon and onto the shaft tips. The three knob shafts stand 0.6 mm taller
than the rest and every tip is chamfered, so P2 drops onto the knob shafts first; they hold it
level while you coax the sensor shafts and the arbors into their holes with tweezers. Screw the
four **M2×5 M-F** standoffs through P2 into the gear standoffs.

*Tools:*

- tweezers
- 4 mm nut driver

*Design review:* [F4: P2 had to find seven shaft tips at once](assembly/FINDINGS.md#f4)

### 6.8 Test: The whole movement, then oil

Repeat the dry run's feel test on the finished movement: two full turns of each thumbwheel
each way, a rock between each pair, and no cross-talk between trains. Then with USB connected
run `hands` while you turn each knob: its hand's reading should change smoothly, by 360° per
1.23 turns of the wheel, and the other two shouldn't move. Run `sweep` once more. Finally add a
small drop of clock oil to each top bearing and the cannon.

*Apply:*

- Check: two full turns each way; `hands` alongside
- Clock oil: one small drop per top bearing
- Clock oil

*Check:*

- Smooth, light turning; about 1° of rock at each pair
- `hands`: the turned train's angle tracks the knob, the other two stay put
- `sweep` still runs cleanly with P2 on

*If it fails:*

- Tighter than on the dry run: P2's bushings pinch a shaft; loosen the hand standoffs a quarter turn and retighten them evenly; if it persists, check that shaft's tip has its chamfer and no burr
- A reading jumps or reverses: the magnet cup has slipped or a magnet isn't diametric; check §5.3
- Otherwise as the dry run (§3.1): swap the binding pair's laser-cut gear for its `_L` spare

## 7. Dial and hands

### 7.1 Dial sticker

Apply the dial sticker to P2, centred on the cannon. The cut-line circle ID is Ø58 mm.
Line up **Hourglass** with the top (12 o'clock) knob.

*Check:* Hourglass points at the 12 o'clock thumbwheel

### 7.2 Hands

The framing hands come blued (spring steel): no finishing. Polish the copper needle. Handle
the hands by the hub; they are thin.

Fit them in this order, each with a dot of Loctite 638 on its arbor and pointing at Hourglass.
The laser-cut **`hand_setting_tool`** does the positioning: press it down over the arbors
until it bottoms, and the hand under it is flush with its own arbor's end.

- Needle on the needle arbor: press with the **one-dot** hole.
- Hand III on arbor III: press with the **two-dot** hole.
- Hand II on arbor II: press with the **three-dot** hole.
- Hand I: push it down arbor I's thin top until it sits on the shoulder.
- The cap: press it with the tool's plain end until the tool touches the top of arbor I.

*Apply:* Loctite 638: a dot on each arbor top before its hand

### 7.3 Test: Hand clearances

Turn each thumbwheel so its hand passes over the other two and the needle, all the way round,
and run `sweep`. Slide a strip of thin paper (about 0.1 mm) between the hands where they
cross: it should pass between every pair without dragging either hand. The needle must not
touch the dial anywhere.

*Apply:* Check: paper between the hands where they cross

*Check:*

- Paper passes between every pair of hands
- No hand or the needle touches the dial or a neighbour anywhere round

*If it fails:*

- Two hands touch: press the lower one down again with the setting tool (it may not have gone fully flush); a bent spring-steel hand can be flattened on glass under a fingertip
- The needle touches the dial: the sticker is lifted at its inner edge, or the needle wasn't pressed fully down with the one-dot hole

## 8. Upper shell, hinge and lid

### 8.1 Upper shell, upside down

Push the two **M1.6×5 countersunk** crystal screws in from outside, then lay the shell upside
down on their heads (they're flush, so it sits flat). Glue a ring of speaker cloth under the
grille slots and epoxy the body closure magnet (top-left, between grille and wall) to the
underside of the top face. Drop the frame spider over the two screws, the crystal into its
pocket and the seat spider on top, then run an **M1.6 nut** down each screw. The crystal stack
is now part of the shell.

*Apply:*

- Contact glue: speaker cloth ring under the grille slots
- 5-minute epoxy: body closure magnet

*Tools:*

- slotted screwdriver 1.5 mm
- 3.2 mm nut driver or tweezers

*Design review:* [F2: Nothing held the crystal and spiders while the shell was turned over and lowered](assembly/FINDINGS.md#f2)

### 8.2 Turn the shell back over

Turn the shell the right way up. The two crystal screws hold the crystal and both spiders in
place.

*Design review:* [F2: Nothing held the crystal and spiders while the shell was turned over and lowered](assembly/FINDINGS.md#f2)

### 8.3 Overlay and lid magnet

Turn the lid over so its inside faces up and epoxy the pierced overlay inside it, keeping the
two hinge holes in the wall clear. Epoxy the lid magnet into the overlay's hole, its pole
attracting the body magnet. Do this before the hinge screws: their tips stand proud of the
inside wall, in the overlay's way.

*Apply:*

- 5-minute epoxy: a thin bead round the rim, clear of the hinge holes
- 5-minute epoxy: lid magnet; poles attract the body magnet

### 8.4 Screw the hinge to the lid

Hold the drilled hinge against the lid's hinge wall, lid upright, and screw the moving leaf on:
two **M1.6×4 DIN 963** screws from outside through the leaf and the laser-cut holes, an M1.6
washer and nut inside each, beside the overlay. Every head must finish flush: when the lid is
fully open the leaves close face to face.

*Tools:*

- slotted screwdriver 1.5 mm
- 3.2 mm nut driver or tweezers

### 8.5 Screw the hinge to the shell

Close the lid onto the shell and screw the fixed leaf on: four **M2×6 DIN 963** screws from
outside through the leaf and the laser-cut wall holes, the laser-cut backing strip and four M2
nuts inside. Bring the strip up against the wall from below: it can't come in sideways past the
crystal spiders.

*Tools:*

- slotted screwdriver 2.5 mm
- 4 mm nut driver

### 8.6 Lower the shell over the movement

Lower the shell over the movement. The thumbwheels must pass through the three notches.
Open the lid and fix the shell with four **M2×6 countersunk** screws through the top face.
Countersunk lengths include the head. These give about **2.37 mm** of thread engagement in
the hand standoffs; the bottom M2×8 screws engage about **2.88 mm** in the bay standoffs.
Check the actual standoffs' usable thread depths before tightening: each screw must clamp
the stack without bottoming out, and all external heads must finish flush.

*Tools:* slotted screwdriver 2.5 mm

*Check:*

- The rim slides on freely before the top screws are tightened
- All external heads flush

### 8.7 Test: Everything that moves, in the case

With the case closed up: turn each thumbwheel through two full turns each way, watching its hand
under the crystal; run `sweep`; press the crown; push a USB-C cable into the wall port; and
press gently on the crown corner while turning knob I.

*Apply:*

- Check: each thumbwheel through its notch
- Check: crown click

*Check:*

- Thumbwheels turn freely in their notches (1.2 mm clearance each side), with the same feel as before
- No hand touches the crystal anywhere round (0.6 mm gap)
- The crown clicks; the USB-C plug goes in straight
- Pressing the crown corner doesn't stiffen knob I

*If it fails:*

- A wheel rubs its notch: loosen the four top screws, centre the shell on the tray and retighten evenly
- A hand touches the crystal: that hand wasn't pressed fully flush (§7.2); lift the shell (four screws) and re-press it
- The crown corner flexes into the train: tighten the corner standoff and gear standoff there; if it still flexes, report it in the design review (F8)

### What holds the two shells together

The overlapping rim is an **alignment skirt with 0.45 mm radial clearance**, not a press-fit
retainer. The fastener path is:

**Four top screws → hand standoffs → P2 → gear standoffs → P1 → three bay standoffs →
three bottom screws through the PCB and nylon spacers.**

At the crown corner, the gear standoff ends in a short **M2×4 F-F standoff under P1**, instead
of a fourth bay standoff, to leave room for the crown switch. That corner is connected through
the plates to the other three floor mounts; it has no direct post to the floor.

For servicing, remove the four top screws and lift off the upper shell and its hinged lid (the
crystal stays in it); leave the three bottom screws fitted unless removing the movement. To lift
the movement out: pull the X27 up through P1 first (its gear can't pass P1's slot), take out the
three bottom screws, lift the frame a little and unplug J4 and J5. No pulling against a friction
fit is intended. Tighten the stack joints snugly without stripping the small brass threads.

The short hex posts and clamped plates are intended to resist sideways motion, but the
CAD checks establish fit, not structural stiffness. The §8.8 test checks the unsupported crown
corner on the prototype. Do not rely on the clearance skirt as rigid bracing.

## 9. Lid

The lid is already hinged and lined (§8).

### 9.1 Test: The lid's travel

Open the lid through its full travel. It passes flat (180°) and stops a little beyond, about
200° with the modelled hinge, when the two leaves close face to face. On a table the lid's far
edge comes to rest on the tabletop first. Close it: the magnets should pull it shut over the
last few millimetres.

*Check:*

- Nothing binds anywhere in the travel
- The leaf screw heads don't touch
- The magnets close it and it sits flat all round

*If it fails:*

- Binds or a head touches: that screw isn't flush; countersink the leaf a little more
- Sits proud at the hinge side: the leaf holes were drilled off the gauge's line; open them 0.2 mm toward the pivot
- Doesn't snap shut: flip the lid magnet (poles repelling)

## 10. Finish and first run

### 10.1 Polish and protect

Polish, then protect the case with Renaissance Wax or a clear lacquer. Unprotected brass will
patina.

### 10.2 Charge, connect and calibrate

1. Charge through the side USB-C port.
2. Triple-click the crown to open the **Alethiometer** Wi-Fi portal. Join it with the password
   you noted in §4, then enter your Wi-Fi, API URL and device key.
3. Click the crown five times to **calibrate**: set all hands to Hourglass and press, set all
   hands to Moon and press, then jog the needle onto Hourglass with knob I and press.
4. Hold the crown, ask your question, release, and watch the needle.

*Apply:*

- Check: charge over USB-C
- Check: triple-click for the Wi-Fi portal

### 10.3 Test: Accuracy

With USB connected and the serial console open: set each hand to four symbols round the dial
(Hourglass, Sun, Moon, Owl) and run `hands` each time; then `needle 0`, `needle 9`,
`needle 18`, `needle 27` and back to `needle 0`, approaching from both sides, and check where it
stops.

*Apply:* Check: `needle 0/9/18/27`, from both sides

*Check:*

- `hands` names the symbol each hand points at, every time
- The needle stops within a quarter of a symbol (2.5°) of each target, from either side

*If it fails:*

- A hand reads the neighbouring symbol at one place only: the AS5600 isn't level or the magnet is off-centre; check §5.3, then recalibrate
- A hand reads off by the same amount everywhere: recalibrate (five clicks)
- The needle is off by the same amount everywhere: recalibrate the needle offset
- The needle lands differently from each side by more than 2.5°: too much backlash in the motor pair; fit the standard needle gear if an `_L` one is in

## 11. Tests and adjustments at a glance

| Where | Test | Passes when | If not |
|---|---|---|---|
| §1.2 | Measure the gears | Tip Ø within +0.06 / −0.10 mm of 27.2 (32T), 15.2 (17T), 28.8 (34T) | Plan on the `_L` spares |
| §1.5 | Bushing pairs | Each drill blank slides through its pair | Release the 638 with heat, redo the pair |
| §3.1 | Dry run | Two full turns each way, even feel, ~1° rock, no cross-talk | Swap the binding pair's laser gear for its `_L` spare |
| §4.3 | Bench test | `hands`, `home`, `sweep`, `tone`, `rec` | pcb/README.md bring-up checklist |
| §6.6 | Motor mesh | `sweep` smooth both ways, a little rock | `_L` needle or motor gear |
| §6.8 | Whole movement | As the dry run; `hands` tracks each knob alone | Even out the hand standoffs; `_L` spare |
| §7.3 | Hand clearances | Paper passes between hands; nothing on the dial | Re-press with the setting tool |
| §8.8 | In the case | Wheels clear the notches, hands clear the crystal, crown corner stiff | Re-centre the shell; re-press a hand |
| §9.1 | Lid | Full travel, flush heads, magnets close it | Countersink more; flip the magnet |
| §10.3 | Accuracy | `hands` right everywhere; needle within 2.5° | Recalibrate; check the sensor |

**The mesh-tuning spares.** Every laser-cut gear has an `_L` twin in the order with teeth 0.16 mm
thinner, marked by a Ø0.5 mm hole in its rim. The design gives each pair 0.22–0.28 mm of backlash at
the pitch circle; a cut whose teeth come out 0.03 mm fat per side still runs, and with the `_L`
gears a worst-case cut (0.065 mm fat per side) does too (`cad/mesh.py`, reported in
`out/build_report.json`). Swap one gear at a time, starting with the laser-cut one in the binding
pair, and only after the dry run says so: the standard gears read more precisely.

**Releasing a Loctite 638 joint.** Hold a soldering iron (about 300 °C) on the part for 20–30 s and
twist it off while hot. Clean both surfaces back to bare metal (a fibreglass pen, then
isopropanol) before refitting with fresh 638.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Fix |
|---|---|
| A knob is stiff | Check the thumbwheel sits flat on its collar and no Loctite reached the sleeve or bushings; the case notch leaves 1.2 mm each side. Then the §3.1 dry-run checks. |
| A hand drags its neighbour | Re-press the lower hand flush with the setting tool (§7.3). |
| Hand reads the wrong symbol near one spot | Check the AS5600 is fully seated in its socket and level on its rest post (chip about 0.7 mm under the magnet), then recalibrate. |
| Something electrical misbehaves | Lift the movement out (§8, *What holds the two shells together*) and probe the labelled test pads (see the [bring-up checklist](pcb/README.md#bring-up-checklist)). Any module can be pulled and swapped. |
| The needle buzzes at the wrong end on wake | Set `MOTOR_PHASE_DIR = -1` in `firmware/src/config.h`. |
| Nothing happens on a crown press | Power switch on (slid toward the USB port)? Check the battery plug polarity and charge it over USB with the switch on. |
| It never speaks | It's muted: four clicks of the crown toggle mute (`status` shows it). Check the J5 plug is fully home. |
